questions.q: What does secret rotation actually accomplish, according to this lesson?
options: It guarantees that a secret can never be leaked in the first place
It limits the window of usefulness of a leaked-but-undetected credential, rather than preventing the leak itself
It makes the secret's value permanently fixed and unchangeable
It removes the need for any access control on the secret
questions.explain: Rotation doesn't stop a leak from happening -- it ensures that a leaked value stops working the next time rotation runs, shrinking how long it stays useful.

questions.q: With a secret rotated every 30 days, what is the maximum window of usefulness for a leaked-but-undetected copy of that secret?
options: Zero days, because rotation prevents the leak from ever occurring
Indefinitely, since rotation does not affect previously leaked copies
At most 30 days, until the next rotation invalidates it
Exactly one year, regardless of the rotation schedule
questions.explain: Rotation on a 30-day schedule means a stolen credential stops working at the next rotation cycle, whether or not the leak was ever detected.

questions.q: What does "least privilege" mean in the context of secret access policies?
options: A secret should be readable only by the specific application or service identity that actually needs it
Secrets should never have any access restrictions at all
Every developer on a team should have read access to all secrets by default
Access policies should be configured once and never reviewed again
questions.explain: Least privilege scopes access to exactly the identity that needs a given secret, rather than granting broad access for convenience.

questions.q: Why is granting an entire team "read all secrets" access a security risk, according to this lesson?
options: Key Vault and Secrets Manager do not support granular access policies at all
It turns one compromised developer account into access to every secret in the vault at once
It has no real downside since teams are always fully trustworthy
It is actually required by Azure and AWS for all production systems
questions.explain: A broad grant means a single compromised identity can reach every secret covered by that grant, instead of just the one it actually needed.

questions.q: How do rotation and least-privilege access policies relate to each other?
options: They are two names for the exact same control
Using one makes the other completely unnecessary
They cover different failure modes: access policies try to prevent an unauthorized read, while rotation assumes a leak slips through anyway and expires it
Access policies only matter after rotation has already failed
questions.explain: A mature secrets practice uses both together -- tightly scoped access to prevent reads, and rotation so an undetected leak still runs out the clock.
